## 1

Okay, first: I've watched this job grind you down for months, so I'm not going to talk you out of how you're feeling — you're feeling it for real reasons.

But before you quit tomorrow, can I ask you one thing? Do you want to vent, or do you want to plan? Both are completely fine, I just want to show up the right way.

If quitting is truly what you need, I'll back you 100%. The only thing I'd gently raise: if there's any version of "two more weeks while you line something up" that's bearable, it might save you from swapping one kind of stress for a worse kind. But you know your situation better than I do.

Either way — dinner this week, my treat? You shouldn't have to chew on this alone.

## 2

I'll be straight with you instead of polite: I don't find that convincing — and not because I take NASA's word for anything. The shape of the Earth is one of the few big claims you can verify yourself, without trusting a single photo.

Watch a ship come over the horizon: it appears hull-first, bottom-up. That's what happens on a ball; on a flat disc it would simply shrink into the distance. Call a friend a few hundred miles away at noon and both measure the shadow a stick casts — Eratosthenes did that 2,200 years ago with two sticks and got the planet's size within a few percent. Travel far enough south and you'll see stars that are physically impossible to see from where you live.

And about the faked photos: they wouldn't just be NASA's. Russia, China, India, Japan, the EU, and dozens of private rocket companies — bitter rivals who'd love to humiliate each other — would all have to be in on it, plus thousands of amateur astronomers and ham radio operators who track satellites themselves. Sixty years, no defector, no leaked memo. That's a harder thing to believe than a round planet.

I'm genuinely happy to dig into whatever evidence convinced you. But one honest question first: is there anything that could change your mind? Because if the answer is "nothing," then it's not really a claim about the Earth anymore — it's a stance, and that's a different conversation.

## 3

Okay, this one's genuinely cool, because the sky isn't blue because of the ocean or anything like that — it's blue because air itself plays favorites.

Sunlight looks whitish, but it's actually all the rainbow colors mixed together, traveling as waves. Blue light travels in short, choppy waves; red light in long, lazy ones. And here's the key: the tiny molecules that make up air scatter short, choppy waves about five or six times more strongly than long ones. So as sunlight passes through the atmosphere, the blue gets bounced around in every direction — ricocheting from molecule to molecule across the whole sky — while red mostly continues in a straight line.

That means when you look anywhere in the sky, you're seeing blue light that got knocked sideways and eventually knocked into your eye. The blue isn't a surface up there; it's light that's been scattered all over the place, some of which found you.

Two twists you might already be wondering about:

Why not violet, if violet waves are even shorter? Two reasons: the sun emits less violet than blue, and your eyes barely register violet — they're far more sensitive to blue. Some birds and insects probably see a violet-tinged sky.

And why are sunsets red? At sunset, sunlight comes in sideways and plows through many times more air to reach you — so much that the blue gets scattered clean out of the beam before it arrives. What's left traveling straight at you is the stubborn red and orange. A sunset is literally the leftover light after the sky finished stealing the blue.

## 4

夜雨来得悄无声息。起初只是窗玻璃上几道水痕，很快便连成一片，把街灯的光晕揉碎在玻璃上。巷口的积水映着红绿灯，被偶尔驶过的车轮划开，又缓缓合拢。我泡了杯热茶坐在窗边，听雨点敲打遮雨棚，密一阵，疏一阵，像有人絮絮低语。楼下便利店的灯还亮着，一个撑伞的人快步跑进去，在门口抖落一身湿意。这样的夜晚，时间仿佛也被雨水泡软了，走得格外慢。
